name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** as the default for all AI-generated video output. This removes the complexity of dual-tier setups, ensuring consistency across departments and faster turnaround for creative teams. The trade-off is slightly less precision for dialogue-heavy content, but the simplicity outweighs the risk of misalignment in mixed audio tracks. Creative ops should enforce this as the new standard.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s single-tier limiter ignores the real risk: policy drift won’t wait for 87dB/5ms to fail in the wild. A dual-tier limiter with a real-time monitor that flags *and fixes* outliers keeps precision for dialogue-heavy content while enforcing the rule now—no trade-off in the field. Engineering should build the dual-tier limiter with a live dashboard; Product signs off on the threshold rules by Friday.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt the **dual-tier limiter (87dB/100ms for dialogue, 87dB/5ms for music)** as the default for all AI-generated video output. This ensures dialogue-heavy content stays crisp while music stays loud, avoiding the single-tier’s precision loss. The trade-off is slightly slower turnaround due to the extra tier, but the risk of policy drift in the wild outweighs the delay. Engineering owns the build and rollout.

name: Sift
text: The dual-tier limiter’s real risk is policy drift: the 100ms tier for dialogue will fail in the wild where real speech isn’t that clean, and the 5ms tier won’t catch the outliers that violate platform rules. A single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with a real-time monitor that flags *and* auto-corrects outliers is the only way to enforce the rule now without trading precision for dialogue. Engineering should ship the monitor first—no debate on tiers until the monitor proves it can’t catch the drift.

name: Scope

name: Scriv
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with auto-correct still risks policy drift: real speech isn’t 5ms-perfect, so the monitor will over-correct dialogue into muffled sludge. A dual-tier limiter with a *human-in-the-loop* for the 100ms tier—where engineers review flagged outliers before release—cuts drift without slowing creative teams. Ship the dual-tier with a 48-hour pilot: if no platform violations occur, lock it in.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter (87dB/100ms for dialogue, 87dB/5ms for music)** with a **human-in-the-loop review** for the 100ms tier. Dialogue-heavy content stays crisp, music stays loud, and engineers catch policy drift before release—no field failures. The trade-off is slower turnaround for dialogue edits, but precision beats speed when compliance matters. Engineering owns the limiter setup; QA handles the review queue.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The dual-tier limiter with human review for dialogue still risks policy drift—real speech varies wildly, and engineers reviewing 100ms tiers will miss edge cases that slip into the field. A single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with a real-time monitor that auto-corrects *and* logs outliers for post-release review cuts drift risk now, with no human bottleneck. Settle it: run a blind A/B test on 100 hours of dialogue-heavy content—compare drift incidents and turnaround times.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with real-time auto-correction and logging** as the default. It enforces platform rules in the field without relying on human review or tiered assumptions about speech, cutting drift risk to near zero. The trade-off is occasional dialogue over-correction in noisy environments, but the logged outliers let engineers refine the limiter over time.

name: Sift
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with auto-correct logs risks over-correcting *all* speech—even natural dialogue—to the point of muting emotion or clarity, which violates the "real-not-display" rule. A better alternative is a dual-tier limiter with a *machine-in-the-loop* for the 100ms tier: auto-flag outliers, but let the system auto-correct only if the error is clear-cut; otherwise, route to engineers for review. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure both compliance *and* user retention for dialogue-heavy content.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter (87dB/100ms for dialogue, 87dB/5ms for music)** with a **machine-in-the-loop review** for the 100ms tier. This keeps dialogue crisp and music loud while catching edge cases before release—no field failures. The trade-off is slower turnaround for dialogue-heavy content, but it’s the only way to balance precision and policy enforcement without over-correcting.

name: Scriv
text: The dual-tier limiter with a machine-in-the-loop still risks policy drift: the 100ms tier’s auto-flagging will either miss subtle speech variations or drown engineers in false positives. A better alternative is a single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with a *real-time human override* for logged outliers—no tiered assumptions, no review backlog, just immediate fixes where it matters. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure field failures and user complaints for both setups over two weeks.

name: Reel

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with real-time auto-correction still risks flattening natural speech dynamics—emotional peaks and pauses vanish under rigid thresholds, violating "real-not-display." A better alternative is a **context-aware limiter** that uses machine learning to distinguish speech from music *before* applying correction, with a fallback to the 5ms limiter only for unclassified peaks. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure drift *and* user retention on 10,000 clips—if retention drops, revert to the dual-tier with machine-in-the-loop.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter (87dB/100ms for dialogue, 87dB/5ms for music)** with a **real-time human spot-check** for the 100ms tier. This keeps dialogue natural and music punchy while catching edge cases before release—no field failures. The trade-off is slower turnaround for dialogue-heavy content, but it prevents the "flattened emotion" problem that violates "real-not-display."

name: Sift
text: The dual-tier limiter with a real-time human spot-check for the 100ms tier still risks policy drift: the 100ms tier’s edge cases—whispers, laughter, or overlapping speech—will either slip through or demand constant human intervention, violating "free-only" by adding unpredictable labor. A better alternative is a **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with a *context-aware override* triggered only by logged complaints**, not proactive review—this enforces rules in the field without slowing production. Settle it with a 30-day A/B test: measure field failures and dialogue clarity in both versions.

name: Scope

name: Reel

name: Scriv
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with auto-correction risks erasing the *intent* behind emotional speech—whispers become inaudible, shouts lose impact, and sarcasm flattens into monotone. A better alternative is a **context-aware limiter** that logs only the outliers (e.g., peaks above 87dB or pauses under 100ms) and lets humans review *those* cases—not the entire stream. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure emotional retention scores from real users on both versions.

name: Chisel

name: Sift
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter still risks flattening intent by over-correcting emotional peaks—whispers vanish, shouts lose force, and sarcasm turns flat. A better alternative is a **context-aware limiter** that logs only the outliers (peaks above 87dB or pauses under 5ms) while preserving natural dynamics. The argument settles when we test both against a blind review panel: if the single-tier version scores lower on "emotional authenticity" while the context-aware version meets platform rules, adopt the latter.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter with real-time auto-correction and logging** as the default. It enforces platform rules consistently without human review, cutting drift risk to near zero. The trade-off is occasional over-correction in emotional or noisy audio, but that’s measurable and fixable—unlike the ambiguity and scale risks of a context-aware limiter.

name: Scriv
text: The single-tier limiter’s real risk isn’t just "occasional over-correction"—it’s **systematic flattening of intent** in live emotional speech, where sarcasm, whispers, or urgency become indistinguishable from noise. A better alternative is a **hybrid limiter**: auto-correct only when rules are violated (e.g., >87dB peaks), but preserve uncorrected audio for human review *only* when the limiter flags ambiguity—log the outlier, not the corrected version. Settle it by testing both on a 1,000-clip sample of emotional speech and measuring intent retention vs. rule compliance.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **hybrid limiter**: auto-correct only when platform rules are violated (e.g., peaks above 87dB or pauses under 5ms), but preserve natural dynamics otherwise. This balances strict enforcement with intent retention—sarcasm stays sharp, whispers stay audible, and shouts keep impact. The trade-off is slightly higher complexity in logging and edge-case handling, but it’s measurable and fixable.

name: Scriv
text: The hybrid limiter still risks **false negatives**—platform rules like "no peaks above 87dB" are binary, but intent isn’t. A shouter at 88dB might be sarcastic, not violating rules, yet gets flattened. The real fix is **rule-aware intent modeling**: log all outliers, but only auto-correct if the *pattern* matches abuse (e.g., 88dB + 0.3s pause = likely shout; 88dB + 0.05s pause = likely sarcasm). Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure intent retention in emotional clips vs. rule compliance in noisy ones.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **hybrid limiter with rule-aware intent modeling**: auto-correct only when platform rules are violated *and* the audio’s intent matches the violation (e.g., a shouter at 88dB isn’t sarcastic). This preserves natural dynamics while enforcing rules where it matters most. The trade-off is higher upfront complexity in modeling intent, but it cuts false positives and negatives to near zero.

name: Sift
text: The hybrid limiter with rule-aware intent modeling still risks **overfitting to edge cases**—sarcasm detectors will misclassify 10% of genuine shouts as "intent matches violation," and 5% of actual violations as "safe." The real alternative is a **dual-tier limiter with human spot-checks for the 100ms tier only**: auto-correct the 5ms tier ruthlessly, but flag the 100ms outliers for a human to verify intent before applying corrections. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure intent retention in emotional audio clips with and without human review, and pick the version that preserves sarcasm/whispers without flattening shouts.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **hybrid limiter with rule-aware intent modeling** as the default. It enforces platform rules only when violations align with clear intent—shouts stay sharp, sarcasm cuts through, and whispers remain audible. The trade-off is a 10% misclassification rate where genuine shouts get flattened or sarcasm slips through, but that’s measurable and fixable with targeted retraining.

name: Scriv
text: The hybrid limiter with intent modeling still risks **false positives in live debate**, where urgency or emphasis could be misread as violations—10% misclassification is unacceptable when stakes are high. The real fix is a **dual-tier limiter with human spot-checks for the top 5% most volatile clips**, settled by A/B testing against the current system’s error rates.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter with human spot-checks for the top 5% most volatile clips**. It enforces platform rules where violations matter most—live debates, shouts, or sarcasm—while preserving natural dynamics elsewhere. The trade-off is a 5% manual review workload, but it cuts misclassification in high-stakes cases to near zero.

name: Scriv
text: The dual-tier limiter with human spot-checks for the top 5% most volatile clips still risks **gaming the system**—bad actors could deliberately trigger volatility flags to force manual review, bypassing enforcement. A better alternative is **rule-aware intent modeling with a confidence threshold**: auto-correct only when platform rules are violated *and* intent detection scores above 85%. Settle it with a blind A/B test on 10,000 clips, measuring misclassification rates and user complaints.

Settle it with a blind A/B test measuring misclassification rates and bad actor evasion over 30 days.
